<p class="breadcrumb-line"><a href="models.html">Models</a> &rsaquo; Clusters and latent variables &rsaquo; Missing data: bounded FIML</p>

Keep partly observed rows instead of deleting them. Part of the
[Models](models.html) collection.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Structure** | X to M to Y, two parallel mediators, or two serial mediators (the saturated graph or the pure chain), each with no, one or two covariates |
| **Class returned** | `FIMLMediationData` (simple), `FIMLParallelMediationData` (parallel) and `FIMLSerialMediationData` (serial) |
| **Route** | `fit_sem(model, data, missing = "fiml", fixed_x = FALSE)` then `extract_mediation()`, or `fit_mediation(engine = "native", engine_args = list(missing = "fiml", ...))` |
| **Standard errors** | observed information, model-based; delta-method effect intervals |
| **Availability** | simple model from 0.16.0; covariates, parallel and serial forms from 0.17.0 |

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(medfit)
library(generics)
```

## What it is, and what it assumes

Ordinary fits delete every row with a missing value on a model variable.
Full-information maximum likelihood (FIML) keeps a row that has at least one
observed model variable and uses what it has. It assumes the variables are
jointly normal and that the missingness is ignorable under that model (missing
at random). It does not impute values, and a fixed pattern of missing values in
a real study is not evidence that missingness is ignorable.

The opt-in is deliberately narrow and explicit. It requires continuous X, M and
Y, independent Gaussian disturbances, free intercepts, `fixed_x = FALSE`,
`meanstructure = TRUE`, observed information and model-based standard errors. A
failed FIML fit never falls back to listwise deletion or to another engine.

## A simple example

```{r}
#| label: fiml-data
d <- withr::with_seed(271L, {
  n <- 400L
  x <- .8 + stats::rnorm(n, sd = 1.1)
  m <- -.4 + .5 * x + stats::rnorm(n, sd = .8)
  y <- .7 + .6 * m + .25 * x + stats::rnorm(n, sd = .9)
  data.frame(treatment = x, mediator1 = m, outcome = y)
})
d$mediator1[seq(1, nrow(d), by = 7)] <- NA_real_
```

```{r}
#| label: fiml-fit
syntax <- "mediator1 ~ a*treatment
outcome ~ b*mediator1 + cp*treatment"
fit <- fit_sem(syntax, d, missing = "fiml", fixed_x = FALSE,
               meanstructure = TRUE, information = "observed", se_type = "model")
nobs(fit)   # every row with an observed model variable is kept
z <- extract_mediation(fit, treatment = "treatment", mediator = "mediator1")
tidy(z, type = "effects")
```

## Which models are covered

| Model | Covariates | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| X, M, Y | 0, 1 or 2 | direct path free or fixed at exactly zero |
| Two parallel mediators | 0, 1 or 2 | the mediator disturbances independent (`M1 ~~ 0*M2`) or free |
| Two serial mediators, saturated | 0, 1 or 2 | both shortcut paths `X -> M2` and `M1 -> Y` written and free |
| Two serial mediators, pure chain | 0, 1 or 2 | both shortcut paths absent; a restriction the data can reject |

In the serial forms all three disturbance covariances (`M1 ~~ 0*M2`,
`M1 ~~ 0*Y`, `M2 ~~ 0*Y`) must be written. With covariates, every covariate
predicts every equation and the exogenous covariances are all written or none. The
syntax rules, parameter counts and the extraction details are in the
[native guide](native-guide.html#bounded-fiml).

In a serial fit, `extract_mediation()` names both mediators in the fitted order.
In the pure chain the treatment is the variable with no path to the second
mediator, so a covariate cannot be named as the treatment there. In the
saturated graph any exogenous variable may be the treatment when no direct path
is fixed, and a direct path fixed at zero marks the treatment. `print()` and
`summary()` of a serial FIML object name the variant and the covariates.

## What is not available

- Case weights, fit tests (`anova()`), profiles and MBCO.
- Source-fit bootstrap intervals: `bootstrap_mediation(source_fit = ...)` is
  implemented but withheld until statistical admission, and raises
  `medfit_error_fiml_inference_unavailable`. Delta-method (normal) intervals from
  `tidy()` and `confint()` are available.
- `quick()`, `pm()` and `glance()` on an extracted FIML object.
- Three or more covariates, three or more mediators, constraints, ties, bounds,
  latent variables, factors and products.

## Evidence

The fits are compared with lavaan raw-data FIML (and OpenMx on one cell per form)
on complete, missing-completely-at-random, missing-at-random and sparse patterns,
with an independent likelihood check and planted-defect tests (the `fiml` and
`fiml-ext` simulation gates). Nothing here is a coverage claim for
intervals under missing data.
